Synchronisation keeps the saved routers, settings, themes, snippets, Docker templates, named workspaces, tunnels and trusted fingerprints alike on all your devices; the passwords and keys of the routers go only if you let them. The data leave the device encrypted with a key made from your password and go where you choose: to a folder a sync client keeps alike, to the folder of the app in a cloud, to a WebDAV or S3 server, to a private Git repository or to your NetworkHelm gateway, and to several of these at once. The service sees neither the data nor the key.
Until you turn synchronisation on, the app sends nothing anywhere.
I have a code from another device
A folder that Syncthing or the client of Dropbox, OneDrive, Yandex Disk, Nextcloud or iCloud Drive keeps alike on your devices. Each device picks the folder itself.
Nextcloud, ownCloud, Synology, Yandex Disk or Mail.ru Cloud, with a password made for this app.
A bucket on MinIO, Yandex Object Storage, Selectel or AWS, with a key for this bucket alone.
A private repository on GitHub, GitLab or Gitea, with a token for this repository alone.
The NetworkHelm gateway on your server; the device gets a token of its own for the login of its page.
A page in a browser reaches a WebDAV or S3 server only if the server lets this page in (CORS).
The gateway lets in the page on GitHub Pages, but a page cannot pin the certificate of the gateway: open the address of the gateway in a tab of this browser first and accept its certificate there.
On a device that synchronises already: Settings → Synchronisation → Show the code. Type here the text under its QR code.

The service holds no NetworkHelm vault yet. Choose the password of synchronisation; you type it once on each new device. Forget it and lose all your devices, and the data cannot be opened: the service has no key.
One of the most common passwords
A run of keys on the keyboard
A sequence such as abcd or 1234
Holds a year or a date
Too easy to guess; a phrase of five words is not

A secret key of 128 bits joins the password. A new device needs it too, from the code of a device that synchronises or typed from paper; a stolen copy of the vault cannot be guessed even with a weak password.
Passwords and keys of the routers
They go encrypted like the rest and lie on the other devices in their protected store. Left off, each device keeps its own.
The keys of synchronisation use software encryption here; its key is kept in the app’s data folder.
The protected storage is unavailable here: synchronisation cannot keep its keys.
Making the key from the password; it takes a few seconds…
The service holds a NetworkHelm vault. Type its password.
The code of the other device opens the vault; the password is not needed.
The code opens the vault on %1$s, where these devices synchronise: %2$s. Join only if they are yours.
The code opens the vault on %1$s; none of its devices has named itself yet. Join only if it is yours.
The key is 26 letters and digits

Write it down and keep it apart from the password. A new device asks for it along with the password, unless it takes the code of a device that synchronises; a device that asks for a new password needs the new key too.
Another copy of the app synchronises this data folder
The code lets another device join without the password. Type the password of synchronisation to show it.
Scan the QR code on the new device or type the text under it there. The code opens all your data: show it to nobody else. It hides in %1$s s.
Turn synchronisation off on this device? The data stay here; the keys and the login of the service leave the device. The files on the service stay.
the keys of synchronisation are not in the protected store of this device: turn synchronisation off and join the vault again

The device stops reading what the others write: the key of the data changes with the password, and its files leave the service. The other devices ask once for the new password; the device turned off keeps what it read before. Revoke its login in the settings of the service itself.
Type the current password, then the new one. The key of the data stays, and the other devices go on without the new password.
Change the key of the data as well

For a password someone else may know: a copy of the vault from before, as the history of the service or a sync client keeps, then opens nothing written after. The other devices ask once for the new password.

Without the current password, whoever uses this device can set a new one; a phone or a tablet asks for its lock first. The key of the data changes with it: every other device stops and asks once for the new password.
Confirm that the device is yours to set a new password of synchronisation without the current one
The vault moves whole, with the same keys. Move the other devices too, or let them take the code of this one.
The vault is copied to one more service with the same keys, and this device keeps every copy up to date. The other devices may add the place too or stay with the one they use.
Each place holds a whole copy of the vault. Devices that use different places get the data of each other through a device that uses both.
Also remove the vault from the service
Every device stops synchronising; the data stay on each of them.
Another device trusts another key for these addresses. This device keeps its own until you pick; keeping it here takes the question to the other devices.
Point the camera at the QR code on the other device.
The camera is not available to the app; type the text under the code instead.
Take a photo of the code
The camera of the phone takes a photo of the QR code on the other device, and the browser reads it.
The browser found no QR code in the photo; take it again, closer and sharper.
